We study space-time symmetries in scalar quantum field theory (including interacting theories) on static space-times. We first consider Euclidean quantum field theory on a static Riemannian manifold, and show that the isometry group is generated by one-parameter subgroups which have either self-adjoint or unitary quantizations. We analytically continue the self-adjoint semigroups to one-parameter unitary groups, and thus construct a unitary representation of the isometry group of the associated Lorentzian manifold. The method is illustrated for the example of hyperbolic space, whose Lorentzian continuation is Anti-de Sitter space.

The study investigates space-time symmetries in scalar quantum field theories, including interacting models, formulated on static space-times. It begins with an analysis of Euclidean quantum field theory on a static Riemannian manifold, where the geometric symmetries are encoded by the manifold’s isometry group.

A central result is that this isometry group can be generated by one-parameter subgroups whose quantum counterparts are represented either by self-adjoint semigroups or by unitary groups. The self-adjoint semigroups correspond to transformations involving Euclidean time, while the unitary groups implement symmetries that preserve the relevant time structure.

By analytically continuing the self-adjoint semigroups from Euclidean to Lorentzian signature, the construction yields one-parameter unitary groups. Together with the unitary symmetries already present in the Euclidean theory, these groups form a unitary representation of the isometry group of the associated Lorentzian space-time. In this way, Lorentzian space-time symmetries are recovered systematically from the Euclidean theory.

The method is illustrated through the example of hyperbolic space. Under analytic continuation, hyperbolic space gives rise to Anti-de Sitter space, allowing the procedure to explicitly connect Euclidean symmetry generators with a unitary representation of the Anti-de Sitter isometry group.

The study investigates how spacetime symmetries arise in scalar quantum field theories defined on static curved spacetimes. It begins with a Euclidean formulation of the theory on a Riemannian manifold equipped with a distinguished time-reflection symmetry. Assuming that the Euclidean measure is invariant under the manifold’s isometries and satisfies reflection positivity, one can apply Osterwalder–Schrader quantization to construct the physical Hilbert space and the corresponding Lorentzian quantum theory.

Euclidean isometries that preserve the chosen positive-time region act naturally on Euclidean field configurations. After quantization, some of these transformations induce unitary operators directly, while those that move the reflection hypersurface generate densely defined self-adjoint operators. Their exponentials initially form local or contractive semigroups rather than globally defined unitary groups. The central step is to analytically continue these self-adjoint semigroups in their parameters. This continuation converts the relevant Euclidean generators into Lorentzian symmetry generators and produces strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups on the physical Hilbert space.

At the Lie-algebra level, the procedure amounts to a Wick rotation of the infinitesimal isometries that reverse sign under Euclidean time reflection. Generators commuting with the reflection remain unchanged, whereas generators that anticommute with it acquire a factor of \(i\). Under appropriate domain, covariance, and integrability conditions, the analytically continued generators satisfy the commutation relations of the Lorentzian isometry algebra. They can then be integrated to obtain a unitary representation of the corresponding Lorentzian isometry group, or of its universal covering group when global topological issues require it.

The construction is illustrated by scalar field theory on hyperbolic space. Choosing a totally geodesic hypersurface as the reflection surface divides hyperbolic space into positive- and negative-time regions and provides the reflection-positive structure needed for quantization. The Euclidean isometry group acts on the field theory, and its quantized generators can be separated according to their behavior under reflection. Analytically continuing the appropriate hyperbolic generators yields the Lie algebra of Anti-de Sitter spacetime. Consequently, the physical Hilbert space carries a unitary representation of the Anti-de Sitter isometry group, with Euclidean translations across the reflection surface continuing into Lorentzian time evolution.

This framework shows that Lorentzian spacetime symmetry need not be imposed independently after quantization. Instead, it can be reconstructed from Euclidean geometric symmetry, reflection positivity, and analytic continuation. The result provides a rigorous connection between Euclidean scalar field theory on static Riemannian manifolds and unitary quantum theories possessing the expected Lorentzian isometries, with the hyperbolic-to–Anti-de Sitter correspondence serving as the principal example.

### Euclidean, Riemannian, and Lorentzian Geometry

Euclidean, Riemannian, and Lorentzian geometries provide different mathematical frameworks for describing space and spacetime.

**Euclidean geometry** is the familiar geometry of flat space. It is based on Euclid’s axioms and uses the standard distance formula. In three dimensions, the squared distance between two nearby points is

\[
ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2.
\]

All directions contribute positively to distance, parallel lines never meet, and the angles of a triangle add up to \(180^\circ\).

**Riemannian geometry** generalizes Euclidean geometry to curved spaces. A Riemannian manifold is equipped with a metric that defines lengths, angles, areas, and curvature locally. Although a curved surface may look approximately Euclidean in a sufficiently small region, its global properties can differ significantly. For example, on a sphere, geodesics—locally shortest paths—are great circles, and the angles of a triangle can add up to more than \(180^\circ\).

**Lorentzian geometry** is closely related to Riemannian geometry but uses a metric with a different signature. Rather than treating every direction in the same way, it distinguishes time from space. In special relativity, the spacetime interval is commonly written as

\[
ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2.
\]

This structure divides intervals into timelike, spacelike, and lightlike categories and gives rise to light cones and causal relationships. Lorentzian geometry is therefore the natural mathematical language of Einstein’s general theory of relativity, in which gravity is interpreted as the curvature of spacetime.

In summary, Euclidean geometry describes flat space, Riemannian geometry describes curved spaces with positive-definite distance measurements, and Lorentzian geometry describes spacetime while incorporating both geometry and causality.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical paragraph explaining how self-adjoint semigroups associated with Euclidean isometries can be analytically continued to unitary groups in interacting scalar QFT.
counterfactuals.output: In an interacting scalar QFT defined by Schwinger functions satisfying the Osterwalder–Schrader axioms, reflection positivity reconstructs a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\) from Euclidean observables supported in a positive-time half-space. Euclidean isometries that preserve this support induce strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroups; in particular, positive Euclidean-time translations act as \(T(\tau)=e^{-\tau H}\), with \(H\ge 0\). The spectral theorem makes \(T(z)=e^{-zH}\) holomorphic for \(\operatorname{Re}z>0\), and its boundary values at \(z=it\) define the unitary real-time evolution \(U(t)=e^{-itH}\). More generally, suitable Euclidean rotations and translations admit analogous continuation of their parameters, yielding unitary boosts and spacetime translations and hence a positive-energy representation of the connected Poincaré group. The argument is nonperturbative and remains valid in the interacting theory because it relies on reflection positivity, Euclidean covariance, regularity, and the spectral condition encoded by the reconstructed generators, rather than on Gaussianity of the Euclidean measure.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a brief academic overview of research on quantizing one-parameter isometry subgroups in static space-times, including an application to the continuation from hyperbolic space to AdS.
counterfactuals.output:
Research on quantizing one-parameter isometry subgroups in static space-times largely combines **Wick rotation**, **reflection positivity**, and the theory of **local symmetric semigroups**. For a static Lorentzian metric  
\[
g_L=-N(x)^2dt^2+h_{ij}(x)\,dx^i dx^j,
\]
one first studies the Riemannian section
\[
g_E=N(x)^2d\tau^2+h_{ij}(x)\,dx^i dx^j.
\]
If the Euclidean field theory or Gaussian measure is invariant under time reflection \(\tau\mapsto-\tau\) and satisfies Osterwalder–Schrader positivity, observables supported in \(\tau>0\) define a physical Hilbert space. Euclidean time translations then descend to a contraction semigroup \(e^{-\tau H}\), whose self-adjoint generator \(H\geq0\) becomes the Lorentzian Hamiltonian through \(e^{-itH}\).

More general one-parameter Euclidean isometry groups need not preserve the positive-time region globally. Their quantization is therefore formulated through **partially defined or local symmetric semigroups**: on suitable support-dependent domains, the Euclidean transformations induce symmetric operators, and self-adjointness or integrability results permit analytic continuation to unitary Lorentzian transformations. At the Lie-algebra level, isometries commuting with reflection quantize directly, whereas reflection-odd generators acquire the usual factor of \(i\). This program extends the Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction framework and the work on local symmetric semigroups associated with Klein, Landau, Fröhlich, Jørgensen, Ólafsson, and others. Important technical issues include domain control, essential self-adjointness, invariance of the Euclidean measure, and global integration from Lie-algebra generators to an isometry-group representation.

A standard application is the continuation of hyperbolic space to anti-de Sitter space. In adapted coordinates,
\[
ds^2_{H^{d+1}}
=d\rho^2+\sinh^2\rho\,d\Omega_{d-1}^2+\cosh^2\rho\,d\tau^2 .
\]
Analytically continuing \(\tau=it\) gives
\[
ds^2_{\mathrm{AdS}_{d+1}}
=d\rho^2+\sinh^2\rho\,d\Omega_{d-1}^2-\cosh^2\rho\,dt^2,
\]
the global static AdS metric, usually interpreted on its universal cover. Reflection positivity across \(\tau=0\) turns the hyperbolic \(\tau\)-translation semigroup into positive-energy AdS time evolution. More generally, continuation of the relevant hyperbolic isometry generators changes the Euclidean real form \(SO(1,d+1)\) into the AdS real form \(SO(2,d)\) of the common complexified Lie algebra. Thus a reflection-positive theory on hyperbolic space can yield a unitary, positive-energy theory on AdS, subject to suitable boundary conditions at conformal infinity and the required self-adjointness assumptions.

counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** We investigate the realization of space-time symmetries in scalar quantum field theory, emphasizing the relation between self-adjoint and unitary quantizations. Starting from the classical action of a real scalar field on symmetric backgrounds, we characterize the conditions under which infinitesimal isometries are represented by essentially self-adjoint operators and exponentiate to unitary representations of the corresponding space-time symmetry group. We then analyze analytic continuation between Euclidean and Lorentzian formulations, clarifying how reflection positivity, spectral properties, boundary conditions, and choices of complex time contour affect the reconstruction of a unitary theory. Particular attention is devoted to Anti-de Sitter space, where the timelike conformal boundary and the nontrivial global structure introduce families of admissible self-adjoint extensions for the wave operator. We relate these extensions to boundary conditions, conserved flux, stability bounds, and unitary representations of the AdS isometry group. The resulting framework identifies when analytic continuation preserves symmetry and unitarity and explains how inequivalent AdS quantizations arise from the interplay among operator domains, boundary data, and global geometry.
